screens.title: Understanding ROS Services
screens.narratorSegment: Services in ROS let nodes ask a direct question and get an answer. In practice you use services for discrete, quick interactions: getting a sensor reading on demand, toggling an LED, or requesting a position change that should complete before the caller continues. This lesson explains the service contract: a name, a request message, and a response message, and shows how to define that contract with a. srv file. You'll see how Python and C++ servers and clients use the same service definitions, how a client blocks until a response arrives, and when a topic or an action would be a better fit. We'll also show the practical developer tools: how to list services, inspect a service's type and arguments, and call a service from the terminal for quick tests. By the end you'll understand the tradeoffs behind synchronous calls and how to design a service that remains fast and reliable. Think about a concrete question your robot might need to answer on demand: how would a service simplify that exchange and what would happen if the call took too long?

keyIdea.text: Services implement a synchronous request-response pattern in ROS, best for short, discrete queries or commands that require an immediate answer.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Understanding ROS Services
Understanding ROS Services
Synchronous request and response for discrete robot commands and queries.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Services give you a contract: a name, a request, and a response. They are ideal for one-off queries such as "What is the battery level?" or discrete commands like toggling an LED. Because clients block while waiting for a response, services are best when the server will answer quickly.
Why this matters
Choosing services for the wrong job causes blocking and latency. Use services for immediate answers; use topics for streaming state and actions for long-running goals.
Concrete example
A /set_led service takes an LED number and a boolean, and returns whether the operation succeeded and a message. This is a short, atomic operation that suits a service perfectly.
Service visual
Client
Sends request, then waits until server replies. Blocking behavior means design carefully.
rosservice call /set_led "led_number: 1 state: true"
Server
Advertises the service, receives request, performs action, returns response.
bool handleSetLed(req, res) –> res.success = true
Explore Key Topics
.srv files
Define request fields above the separator and response fields below it.
Clients & Servers
Implementations in Python and C++ use the same compiled message bindings.
rosservice tools
List, inspect, and call services directly from the terminal for fast testing.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn four practical skills that let you build and debug ROS services. First, you will distinguish topics, services, and actions and know which pattern fits a given problem. Second, you'll write service servers in both Python and C++, implementing callbacks that receive a typed request and return a typed response. Third, you'll create service clients in both languages that wait for a service to appear, send a request, and handle the blocking return. Fourth, you'll use rosservice command-line tools to list services, inspect their types and arguments, and call them from the terminal for quick tests. Each objective is grounded with a concrete example: an LED toggle service, a sum computation service, and a test workflow using rosservice call. You'll practice cross-language interoperability to confirm that Python clients can call C++ servers and vice versa. These skills matter because services are a fundamental synchronous pattern in ROS; writing robust servers and clients and testing them from the terminal helps you debug robot behavior faster and design non-blocking systems when necessary.

screens.title: Hands-on Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson includes a hands-on activity where you create a ComputeSum. srv, implement a Python server that returns the sum, and write a Python client to request the sum of 5 and 3. screens.title: What is a ROS Service?
screens.narratorSegment: A ROS service is a named contract that defines how one node requests data or an action and how another node responds. The contract consists of a service name and two message types: request and response. Requests carry the input data, like an LED number and desired on/off state; responses carry the result, such as a success flag and a message. Services follow a client-server model: a server advertises the service name to the ROS master, and any client can call that name. The important behavioral point is that clients block while waiting for the server to respond. That blocking makes services ideal for short, deterministic operations where the caller must wait. A common misconception is to use services for high-frequency telemetry; that is not recommended because repeated blocking calls create latency and can destabilize real-time behavior. Instead, stream continuous state on a topic. As an example, a /set_led service should toggle an LED and immediately return success or failure. Think of a service as a telephone call: you ask a direct question and you wait on the line for the answer. The takeaway: use services for discrete, short exchanges that must complete before the caller proceeds.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Services are synchronous request-response interactions best used for short, discrete operations that need an immediate reply.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What is a ROS Service?
Service definition
A service pairs a request type with a response type under a common name. It is synchronous: the client waits for the server to return.
• Name: the identifier nodes call, e.g. /set_led.
• Request: typed fields sent by the client.
• Response: typed fields returned by the server.
# Example .srv (contract) int32 led_number bool state --- bool success string message
Common mistake
Using services for high-rate telemetry. If you need continuous updates, use a topic to avoid repeated blocking calls.
Analogy: telephone call
You ask a specific question and wait on the line for the answer. The conversation ends when the server responds.
Client (caller)
Blocks until response. Uses wait_for_service and a ServiceProxy or serviceClient.
Example: ask "set LED 1 to true" and wait for success.
Server (answerer)
Advertises the service, runs a callback that processes the request and returns a response object.
Example: receive led_number and state, toggle hardware, return success and message.
Key Takeaway

Services are for quick, blocking calls where the client must wait for a result.

Check your understanding
If your node needs updates at 100 Hz, would you use a service? Why or why not?

screens.title: Service message contract (.srv files)
screens.narratorSegment: A. srv file defines the exact contract between client and server. It is split into two parts by a separator line: request fields on top and response fields below. This file lives in the srv/ directory of your package and is compiled into language-specific message classes used by both Python and C++. For example the SetLed. srv includes an int32 led_number and a bool state in the request, and a bool success and a string message in the response. When you change a. srv file you must add it to add_service_files() in CMakeLists. txt and regenerate messages so each language gets updated bindings. A common pitfall is forgetting to re-run the build or not listing the. srv in package configuration, which results in missing symbols at compile time. Use rosservice type and rosservice args to confirm the compiled service type and argument names are what you expect. The key practical skill is thinking of the. srv as an A P I contract: keep fields minimal, avoid large payloads, and choose clear names so clients and servers remain compatible across languages.

keyIdea.title: .srv contract
keyIdea.text: .srv files define request and response fields. They are the single source of truth for cross-language service bindings.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Service message contract
Structure of a .srv file
The top section lists request fields; a line with three dashes separates the response section.
# File: srv/SetLed.srv int32 led_number bool state --- bool success string message
• Place small, atomic fields only. Large binary payloads are better handled by topics or storage.
• Treat the file as an API contract shared by all languages and nodes.
• After editing, add the file to add_service_files() and re-run message generation.
Build tip
Include message_generation and add_service_files() in CMakeLists.txt, then call catkin_make or colcon to generate language bindings.
Process flow
1. Define .srv
Add request and response fields in srv/ and commit changes.
2. Register in build
Add the file to add_service_files() and list dependencies for message_generation.
3. Build and generate
Run your workspace build so the service types are available in Python and C++.
4. Use and test
Implement servers and clients, then test with rosservice call and rosservice args/type.
Key Takeaway

The .srv file is the single source of truth for service messages and must be compiled for all language bindings.

screens.title: Python: Writing a Service Server
screens.narratorSegment: Writing a Python service server with rospy follows a clear pattern: initialize a node, define a callback that receives a typed request and returns a typed response, advertise the service, and spin. The callback is where you perform the requested action—toggle hardware, compute a value, or query state—and then construct and return the appropriate response object. In the SetLed example the callback logs the incoming LED number and state, performs the operation, and returns a SetLedResponse containing success and a message string. Remember that the server runs in the node's thread and should avoid long blocking operations. If a handler must perform long work, spawn a worker thread or convert the interaction to an action so the client isn't forced to block. When testing, use rosservice call to validate the server before writing client code: that isolates server logic from client issues. Finally, include logging so you can confirm the server received the request and returned the response. This makes debugging cross-language interactions much simpler. Python: Writing a Service Server means create a callback returning the response type, advertise with rospy.service, and keep work short to avoid freezing clients.. In practical terms, implementing a rospy server that handles requests and returns responses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Python server pattern
keyIdea.text: Create a callback returning the response type, advertise with rospy.Service, and keep work short to avoid freezing clients.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Python Service Server
Server structure
Init node, define handler, advertise service, spin.
#!/usr/bin/env python3 import rospy from my_first_robot.srv import SetLed, SetLedResponse def handle_set_led(req): rospy.loginfo("Setting LED %d to %s", req.led_number, req.state) # Here you would actually control the LED hardware success = True message = "LED %d set to %s" % (req.led_number, req.state) return SetLedResponse(success, message) if __name__ == '__main__': rospy.init_node('led_server') srv = rospy.Service('/set_led', SetLed, handle_set_led) rospy.loginfo("LED server is ready.") rospy.spin()
Example
Callback receives req and returns SetLedResponse(success, message).
Pitfall
Avoid long blocking work in the callback or clients will freeze while waiting.
Testing tips
  • Run the server, then call rosservice list to verify the name is advertised.
  • Use rosservice info /set_led and rosservice args to confirm the generated type and fields.
  • Call rosservice call with the appropriate YAML block to confirm a response before running a client program.
Key Takeaway

Keep server callbacks short and well-logged; test with rosservice call to isolate server logic.

screens.title: Python: Writing a Service Client
screens.narratorSegment: A Python client uses a simple, synchronous pattern: wait for the service to become available, create a proxy or callable object, and invoke it like a local function. The call blocks until the server returns a response. The example client uses rospy. wait_for_service to ensure the server is advertised, then constructs a ServiceProxy for /set_led with the SetLed type. Calling the proxy returns a response object from which you can read fields like success and message. Wrap the call in a try/except to catch ServiceException, which happens if the call fails. A common misconception is assuming the proxy is non-blocking; it is blocking by design. If you need asynchronous behavior or progress feedback for long-running work, use actions instead. For test-driven development, first validate the server with rosservice call, then run the client; this isolates errors between server and client code. Also, log the response in the client so you can verify the server's return values during debugging. In practical terms, wait_for_service, serviceproxy, and handling the blocking call. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Client pattern
keyIdea.text: Use wait_for_service then ServiceProxy to call the service. Expect the call to block until a response is returned.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Python Service Client
Client pattern
Wait for availability, create proxy, call and handle response or exception.
#!/usr/bin/env python3 import rospy from my_first_robot.srv import SetLed def set_led_client(led_number, state): rospy.wait_for_service('/set_led') try: set_led = rospy.ServiceProxy('/set_led', SetLed) resp = set_led(led_number, state) return resp.success, resp.message except rospy.ServiceException as e: rospy.logerr("Service call failed: %s", e) return False, "Error" if __name__ == '__main__': rospy.init_node('led_client') success, message = set_led_client(1, True) rospy.loginfo("Result: %s - %s", success, message)
Use try/except around the blocking call so failures don't crash your node. Log the returned fields to confirm server behavior.
Misconceptions
Calling a service frequently to poll state is not ideal because each call blocks. Prefer topics for frequent updates. For long-running operations, prefer actions to receive feedback and keep clients responsive.
Key Takeaway

ServiceProxy calls look like local calls but block until the response arrives; handle exceptions and avoid using them as a high-rate polling mechanism.

The main function initializes the node and calls advertiseService with the service name and handler. Then ros::spin keeps the server available. Unlike Python, the callback in C++ receives references you populate directly, and the return value signals whether the service succeeded. Important practical notes: keep handlers short, log key steps with ROS_INFO for visibility, and ensure your CMakeLists. txt includes message_generation and links generated message headers so the service types are available at compile time. When testing, you can call the C++ server with a Python client to verify cross-language bindings—this proves the. srv contract was compiled correctly and messages serialize across the ROS transport layer without language-specific code. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › C++ Service Server
Server pattern in C++
Advertise the service, implement a handler that fills the response and returns a bool.
#include <ros/ros.h> #include <my_first_robot/SetLed.h> bool handleSetLed(my_first_robot::SetLed::Request& req, my_first_robot::SetLed::Response& res) { ROS_INFO("Setting LED %d to %d", req.led_number, req.state); res.success = true; res.message = "LED set successfully"; return true; } int main(int argc, char** argv) { ros::init(argc, argv, "led_server"); ros::NodeHandle nh; ros::ServiceServer service = nh.advertiseService("/set_led", handleSetLed); ROS_INFO("LED server is ready."); ros::spin(); return 0; }
Return true from your handler for success and fill response fields directly. Use ROS_INFO to log requests and results for easier debugging with rosservice tools.
Build notes
  • Add service files to add_service_files() and include message_generation in CMakeLists.
  • Link against the generated message targets so headers compile.
  • Confirm svc symbols are present by running catkin_make or colcon build.
Pro tip
If your C++ server compiles but the service is not listed, check that you added the .srv file to the build and that the workspace recompiled messages.

The example shows a straightforward client that requests LED number and state, calls the server, and prints the result. Remember to test the server first using rosservice call so you isolate failures. A subtle point is that the network wiring and generated message types must match: mismatched. srv definitions or stale builds cause runtime failures. If your client call returns false, verify the service is advertised and that both sides use the compiled message definitions from the same workspace. This cross-language compatibility is a major advantage of ROS: once the. srv is compiled, Python and C++ can exchange messages seamlessly over the ROS transport. screens.title: Topics vs. Services vs. Actions
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right ROS communication pattern depends on directionality, duration, and the need for feedback. Topics are publish-subscribe streams best for continuous data like sensor readings; they are one-way and non-blocking. Services are synchronous request-response interactions suited for quick queries or commands that must complete before the caller proceeds. Actions are for long-running goals that need feedback and cancellation; they are asynchronous and return a result plus progress updates. A helpful mental model: topics are one-way highways, services are two-way streets, and actions are a long journey with periodic check-ins. A common error is using a service to poll frequent state—this causes the caller to block repeatedly, introducing jitter. For example, calling /get_battery_level every 100 ms is a poor design; publish battery level on a topic at 1 Hz and subscribe in interested nodes. When you need to request an immediate change and want immediate confirmation, use a service. For a move-to-position that may take seconds and require feedback and cancellation, use an action. The right choice keeps your robot responsive and predictable. Topics vs. Services vs. Actions means use topics for continuous streams, services for short blocking queries/commands, and actions for long-running, cancelable goals.. In practical terms, choose the right communication pattern for the job. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Topics vs Services vs Actions
Which pattern to use?
Compare direction, blocking behavior, and typical use cases to decide.
Topics
Publish-subscribe, one-way, non-blocking. Best for sensors and streaming state.
Example: battery level published at 1 Hz to /battery_level.
Services
Request-response, two-way, blocking client. Best for quick queries and atomic commands.
Example: /set_led toggles LED and returns success immediately.
Actions
Goal-feedback-result, asynchronous, non-blocking client. Best for long-running tasks requiring feedback or cancellation.
Example: move to position with continuous feedback and the option to cancel.
Design pitfall
Calling a service at high frequency to poll data will block the caller and create jitter. Use topics for frequent updates.
Key Takeaway
Match the communication pattern to the temporal needs of your task: streaming, immediate answer, or long-running goal.

Use rosservice info /service_name to show which node provides the service and the service type. rosservice type returns the message type for the service, and rosservice args shows the request field names. The most powerful debug tool is rosservice call: provide a YAML-ish payload for the request and observe the response. This helps you test server logic before writing client code and speeds debugging across language boundaries. screens.title: Blocking Behavior and Performance
screens.narratorSegment: Services intentionally block the calling thread until the server responds. This guarantees a synchronous exchange but also means the client must be designed to tolerate that pause. If the server takes too long, the client node stalls and can introduce latency across the system. When designing services, keep handlers short and deterministic. If you foresee longer operations, either offload work to background threads inside the server or switch to actions so the client receives progress updates and can cancel. Another design pattern is to turn polling into subscriptions: instead of calling a service repeatedly to check state, publish the state on a topic and let subscribers last known value. A real-world example: querying battery level every 100 ms via a service is a poor design because the caller will block frequently. Prefer a battery-level topic published at an appropriate rate. Always consider responsiveness and failure modes: build timeouts, exception handling, and graceful degradation to maintain robust robot behavior under network hiccups or crashed servers. Blocking Behavior and Performance means because clients block, design handlers to be fast or use asynchronous patterns (actions or worker threads) for long work.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Blocking and performance
Understand the runtime cost of blocking and design accordingly.
Why blocking matters
Clients pause until the server replies. Frequent calls or slow handlers create delays and jitter that affect control loops.
Alternatives
Use topics for streaming state; use actions for long tasks that require feedback and cancellation; spawn threads for longer server work.
Assessment scenario
A navigation node calls /get_battery_level every 100 ms. Is this a good design? No — it blocks frequently. Publish battery level on a topic instead to keep navigation responsive.
Key Takeaway
Design services for short, fast work. If not possible, use asynchronous alternatives to preserve responsiveness.

fullNarratorScript:
Services in ROS let nodes ask a direct question and get an answer. In practice you use services for discrete, quick interactions: getting a sensor reading on demand, toggling an LED, or requesting a position change that should complete before the caller continues. This lesson explains the service contract: a name, a request message, and a response message, and shows how to define that contract with a. srv file. You'll see how Python and C++ servers and clients use the same service definitions, how a client blocks until a response arrives, and when a topic or an action would be a better fit. We'll also show the practical developer tools: how to list services, inspect a service's type and arguments, and call a service from the terminal for quick tests. By the end you'll understand the tradeoffs behind synchronous calls and how to design a service that remains fast and reliable. Think about a concrete question your robot might need to answer on demand: how would a service simplify that exchange and what would happen if the call took too long?

In this chapter you will learn four practical skills that let you build and debug ROS services. First, you will distinguish topics, services, and actions and know which pattern fits a given problem. Second, you'll write service servers in both Python and C++, implementing callbacks that receive a typed request and return a typed response. Third, you'll create service clients in both languages that wait for a service to appear, send a request, and handle the blocking return. Fourth, you'll use rosservice command-line tools to list services, inspect their types and arguments, and call them from the terminal for quick tests. Each objective is grounded with a concrete example: an LED toggle service, a sum computation service, and a test workflow using rosservice call. You'll practice cross-language interoperability to confirm that Python clients can call C++ servers and vice versa. These skills matter because services are a fundamental synchronous pattern in ROS; writing robust servers and clients and testing them from the terminal helps you debug robot behavior faster and design non-blocking systems when necessary.

This lesson includes a hands-on activity where you create a ComputeSum. srv, implement a Python server that returns the sum, and write a Python client to request the sum of 5 and 3. Then you will write equivalent C++ server and client implementations and test cross-language operation. The key learning outcome is that service message definitions are language-agnostic: once compiled, clients and servers in different languages can exchange requests and responses without extra translation. The exercise also teaches a practical test flow: first use rosservice call to verify the server responds correctly, then run the client node to confirm programmatic use. You will log results in the server and print the response in the client to confirm behavior. This sequence trains you to debug services incrementally and to recognize when a service is the right tool versus a topic or an action.

A ROS service is a named contract that defines how one node requests data or an action and how another node responds. The contract consists of a service name and two message types: request and response. Requests carry the input data, like an LED number and desired on/off state; responses carry the result, such as a success flag and a message. Services follow a client-server model: a server advertises the service name to the ROS master, and any client can call that name. The important behavioral point is that clients block while waiting for the server to respond. That blocking makes services ideal for short, deterministic operations where the caller must wait. A common misconception is to use services for high-frequency telemetry; that is not recommended because repeated blocking calls create latency and can destabilize real-time behavior. Instead, stream continuous state on a topic. As an example, a /set_led service should toggle an LED and immediately return success or failure. Think of a service as a telephone call: you ask a direct question and you wait on the line for the answer. The takeaway: use services for discrete, short exchanges that must complete before the caller proceeds.

A. srv file defines the exact contract between client and server. It is split into two parts by a separator line: request fields on top and response fields below. This file lives in the srv/ directory of your package and is compiled into language-specific message classes used by both Python and C++. For example the SetLed. srv includes an int32 led_number and a bool state in the request, and a bool success and a string message in the response. When you change a. srv file you must add it to add_service_files() in CMakeLists. txt and regenerate messages so each language gets updated bindings. A common pitfall is forgetting to re-run the build or not listing the. srv in package configuration, which results in missing symbols at compile time. Use rosservice type and rosservice args to confirm the compiled service type and argument names are what you expect. The key practical skill is thinking of the. srv as an A P I contract: keep fields minimal, avoid large payloads, and choose clear names so clients and servers remain compatible across languages.

Writing a Python service server with rospy follows a clear pattern: initialize a node, define a callback that receives a typed request and returns a typed response, advertise the service, and spin. The callback is where you perform the requested action—toggle hardware, compute a value, or query state—and then construct and return the appropriate response object. In the SetLed example the callback logs the incoming LED number and state, performs the operation, and returns a SetLedResponse containing success and a message string. Remember that the server runs in the node's thread and should avoid long blocking operations. If a handler must perform long work, spawn a worker thread or convert the interaction to an action so the client isn't forced to block. When testing, use rosservice call to validate the server before writing client code: that isolates server logic from client issues. Finally, include logging so you can confirm the server received the request and returned the response. This makes debugging cross-language interactions much simpler. Python: Writing a Service Server means create a callback returning the response type, advertise with rospy.service, and keep work short to avoid freezing clients.. In practical terms, implementing a rospy server that handles requests and returns responses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Python client uses a simple, synchronous pattern: wait for the service to become available, create a proxy or callable object, and invoke it like a local function. The call blocks until the server returns a response. The example client uses rospy. wait_for_service to ensure the server is advertised, then constructs a ServiceProxy for /set_led with the SetLed type. Calling the proxy returns a response object from which you can read fields like success and message. Wrap the call in a try/except to catch ServiceException, which happens if the call fails. A common misconception is assuming the proxy is non-blocking; it is blocking by design. If you need asynchronous behavior or progress feedback for long-running work, use actions instead. For test-driven development, first validate the server with rosservice call, then run the client; this isolates errors between server and client code. Also, log the response in the client so you can verify the server's return values during debugging. Python: Writing a Service Client means use wait_for_service then serviceproxy to call the service. expect the call to block until a response is returned.. In practical terms, wait_for_service, serviceproxy, and handling the blocking call. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A C++ service server uses the advertiseService A P I on a NodeHandle to register a handler function that takes request and response references. In the example the handler receives my_first_robot::SetLed::Request and Response references. It fills response fields and returns true to indicate success. The main function initializes the node and calls advertiseService with the service name and handler. Then ros::spin keeps the server available. Unlike Python, the callback in C++ receives references you populate directly, and the return value signals whether the service succeeded. Choosing the right ROS communication pattern depends on directionality, duration, and the need for feedback. Topics are publish-subscribe streams best for continuous data like sensor readings; they are one-way and non-blocking. Services are synchronous request-response interactions suited for quick queries or commands that must complete before the caller proceeds. Actions are for long-running goals that need feedback and cancellation; they are asynchronous and return a result plus progress updates. A helpful mental model: topics are one-way highways, services are two-way streets, and actions are a long journey with periodic check-ins. A common error is using a service to poll frequent state—this causes the caller to block repeatedly, introducing jitter. For example, calling /get_battery_level every 100 ms is a poor design; publish battery level on a topic at 1 Hz and subscribe in interested nodes. When you need to request an immediate change and want immediate confirmation, use a service. For a move-to-position that may take seconds and require feedback and cancellation, use an action. The right choice keeps your robot responsive and predictable. Services intentionally block the calling thread until the server responds. This guarantees a synchronous exchange but also means the client must be designed to tolerate that pause. If the server takes too long, the client node stalls and can introduce latency across the system. When designing services, keep handlers short and deterministic. If you foresee longer operations, either offload work to background threads inside the server or switch to actions so the client receives progress updates and can cancel. Another design pattern is to turn polling into subscriptions: instead of calling a service repeatedly to check state, publish the state on a topic and let subscribers last known value. A real-world example: querying battery level every 100 ms via a service is a poor design because the caller will block frequently. Prefer a battery-level topic published at an appropriate rate. Always consider responsiveness and failure modes: build timeouts, exception handling, and graceful degradation to maintain robust robot behavior under network hiccups or crashed servers.
